chunks: And what Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Ibn Abi Umayr from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) that he said:

Regarding a man who did not stand at Al-Muzdalifah and did not spend the night there until he went to Mina, he said: 'Did he not see the people? They did not hasten to Mina when they entered it.' I said: 'Indeed, he was ignorant of that.' He said: 'He should return.' I said: 'Indeed, that has already passed him.' He said: 'There is no harm.'

The explanation in these two narrations, although their origin is Muhammad ibn Yahya Al-Khas'ami, and that he narrates it once from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) without an intermediary and once with an intermediary, is that whoever has stood at Al-Muzdalifah for a short time, that has sufficed him. And what is meant by his saying 'he did not stand at Al-Muzdalifah' is the complete standing, which when a person performs it, it is more perfect and superior, and when he does not stand in that manner, it is less in reward, although it does not invalidate the Hajj, because the short standing suffices there in case of necessity. And that which indicates this is what he narrated:

key_terms.الْمُزْدَلِفَة: Muzdalifah, a plain near Mecca where pilgrims gather after leaving Mina
key_terms.الْوُقُوف: Standing, a ritual act of remaining in a specific place during Hajj
key_terms.لَا بَأْسَ: There is no harm (it is permissible/valid)
key_terms.مِنًى: Mina, a valley and site of Hajj rituals near Mecca

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling if a pilgrim does not spend the night at Muzdalifah?
ai.summary: In *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Shaykh al-Tusi records this narration from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) to clarify the distinction between the essential pillar (*rukn*) of standing at Muzdalifah and its recommended perfection (*kamal*). The Imam establishes that while spending the night is ideal, a brief presence suffices for validity (*ibaha*), reflecting the Shia juristic principle of accommodating necessity (*darurah*) without invalidating the Hajj. This ruling underscores the flexibility within Shia fiqh regarding ritual completeness versus strict obligation.
